slides.subtitle: FM 3-09 (12 August 2024): key ideas for junior Soldiers

slides.title: FM 3-09 at a glance

purpose.text: The Army's field manual for fire support and field artillery operations.

applies_to.text: Regular Army, Army National Guard and Army Reserve, unless the manual says otherwise.

stats.label: danger close distance for mortars or artillery

slides.title: What this means for you

items.text: Forward observers locate targets accurately, then call for and adjust fire support.
Danger close: rounds from mortars or artillery predicted to land within 600 meters of friendly troops.
Fires that are not pre-cleared or allowed by a permissive measure must be positively cleared.
In a no-fire area, fires or their effects are prohibited.
The sun must never be viewed through the telescope without a sun filter.

slides.title: What changed from the 2020 edition

items.text: Formally recognizes multidomain operations and its tenets.
Lines up with FM 3-0 on competition, crisis and armed conflict.
Changes several fire support terms and definitions, including danger close.
Introduces the operational fires command.
Adds a large-scale combat battlefield framework figure in chapter 6.
Adds a maritime section to the appendix on environment and terrain.

slides.title: Foundations of Fire Support

blurb.text: Fire support brings fires, target acquisition, and attack systems together to support the commander's plan.

slides.title: Fire support: what it is and what field artillery does

statement.text: Fire support brings indirect fires, target acquisition, armed aircraft, and other attack systems together against targets to support the commander's plan.

points.text: The fire support system's elements: command and control, target acquisition, and attack/delivery systems.
Field artillery's role: destroy, neutralize, or suppress the enemy by cannon, rocket, and missile fire, and integrate all fire support into operations.
Fire support must always be conducted in the spirit of the offense, even in the defense.

slides.title: Who trains you

duties.text: Train and resource training one echelon down, and evaluate two echelons down.
Primary trainers of their elements. Example: a platoon leader is responsible for the platoon's training and performance.
Train individuals, crews, and small teams; advise commanders on all aspects of training.
Keep training focused on sustaining strengths and improving weaknesses.

slides.title: The Fire Support System

blurb.text: Fire support works as a system with three parts: command and control, target acquisition, and attack and delivery.

slides.title: Fire support people at company and platoon

duties.text: The fire support representative for the maneuver platoon.
Main job: locate targets accurately, then call for and adjust fire support.
The FO must fully understand their part in the observation plan.
Senior enlisted assistant to the company fire support officer; does that officer's duties when they are absent.
Trains the fire support team and the forward observers.
Works for the company or troop commander in combat.
Writes the fire support plan from the commander's guidance and submits it for approval.
A certified Service member who requests, controls and adjusts surface-to-surface fires.
Cannot control close air support attacks and does not replace a joint terminal attack controller (JTAC).

talking_points.text: The fire support sergeant also advises the fire support officer on tasking joint fires observers and other observers.

slides.title: The fire support team (FIST)

statement.text: Each maneuver company or troop gets a field artillery team that plans and coordinates all the fires supporting it.

points.text: Those fires include mortars, field artillery, naval surface fire support and close air support.
The FIST works closely with the battalion and brigade fire support elements.
Infantry and armor company FISTs make artillery, mortar and joint fire support work for the maneuver force.

slides.title: Target or suspected target?

points.text: Targets must meet accuracy and timeliness requirements for engagement.
Suspected targets must be confirmed before any engagement.

talking_points.text: Target selection standards are the criteria used to decide whether enemy activity is a target.
Target acquisition ranges from Soldiers who see the target to advanced electronic sensors.

slides.title: Fire Support and the Operations Process

blurb.text: This chapter covers the fire support functions, targeting and coordination, rehearsals, execution, and assessment.

slides.title: Danger close: the distances to know

stats.label: Mortars or artillery: impact within this of friendly troops
Naval surface fires: impact within this of friendly troops
Largest creeping adjustment: mortars or artillery
Largest creeping adjustment: naval surface fire support

talking_points.text: Danger close is a mandatory call. It warns that the closest friendly troops are at higher risk from where the weapon impacts.
The creeping fire method of adjustment will be used exclusively during danger close missions.
Do not confuse the creeping fire method with risk-estimate distances or minimum safe distances.

slides.title: The targeting cycle: decide, detect, deliver, assess

steps.label: Decide
steps.detail: Start identifying high-payoff targets.

steps.label: Detect
steps.detail: Carry out the information collection plan.

steps.label: Deliver
steps.detail: Carry out fire support tasks as the attack guidance matrix lays out.

steps.label: Assess
steps.detail: Combat assessment: battle damage assessment, munitions effectiveness assessment, and reattack recommendation.

talking_points.text: Targeting means selecting and prioritizing targets and matching the right response to each target.
Targeting happens continuously throughout an operation.

slides.title: Fratricide: stopping friendly-fire casualties

statement.text: Fratricide is killing or wounding friendly or neutral people by accident with friendly fire.

points.text: If enemy and friendly forces could be intermixed in the target area, units must positively verify their identity after detection, before engaging.
Fratricides can occur when fire support coordination measures (FSCMs) are not used and not shared with units.
Take special caution when daytime visibility is limited and at night.

talking_points.text: Marking devices such as thermal beacons, thermal tape, and navigational aids help tell friend from foe.
Fratricide can also happen in training and simulations, not just in combat.

slides.title: Positive clearance of fires: what it takes

items.text: Fires that are not pre-cleared or allowed by a permissive FSCM must be positively cleared.
This should be a battle drill in command posts. Best method: send the call for clearance over two nets, the fire support net and the maneuver net.
Best available method of locating the target.
Positive identification of the target as enemy.
Eyes on the target, if possible.
Clearance from the right outside elements if the target is outside unit boundaries.
Coordination with airspace users affected by the munition's flight path.

talking_points.text: For positive clearance of fires, the listed items should be obtained.
Clearance of fires makes sure fires or their effects have no unintended consequences on friendly units or the scheme of maneuver.

slides.title: The four parts of an essential fire support task

steps.label: Task (what)
steps.detail: The effect fires must have on an enemy formation's function or capability. Enemy oriented.

steps.label: Purpose (why)
steps.detail: The benefit to the supported commander. Friendly oriented.

steps.label: Method (how)
steps.detail: How the target is engaged, using priority, allocation and restrictions.

steps.label: Effect (result)
steps.detail: The quantified, observable result of successfully doing the task.

talking_points.text: An essential fire support task is a critical element of the fire support plan that must be accomplished for mission success.
Each essential fire support task will be described in the sequence of planned execution using task, purpose, method, effects.

slides.title: Permissive vs. restrictive fire support coordination measures

talking_points.text: These measures will change frequently during large-scale combat operations.

points.text: They make it easier to attack targets.
Fires must be cleared with both terrain owners and other airspace users.
Free-fire area: any weapon system may fire into it without more coordination with the headquarters that set it up.
They provide safeguards for friendly forces and noncombatants, facilities, or terrain.
No-fire area: fires or their effects are prohibited inside it.
Restrictive fire area: fires that exceed its restrictions will not be delivered without coordination with the headquarters that set it up.

slides.title: Lines on the map and what they mean for fires

talking_points.text: A coordinated fire line is not authorization to fire indiscriminately into the area.
A restrictive fire line keeps converging friendly forces from hitting each other or engaging the same targets twice.

cells: Coordinated fire line (CFL)
Surface fires may fire beyond it at any time without more coordination.
Inside the setting unit's boundaries; must still follow the rules of engagement.
Fire support coordination line (FSCL)
All fires must be coordinated with affected commanders before engaging.
Short of it, all fires must be coordinated with the commander who set it.
Restrictive fire line (RFL)
Fires or their effects are prohibited from crossing it.
Set between friendly forces moving toward each other, to prevent fratricide.
Boundary
Units normally do not fire across adjacent or forward boundaries.
Unless coordinated with the affected unit or allowed by a measure like a CFL.

slides.title: Can fires go into a no-fire area?

nodes.text: Has the headquarters that set the no-fire area approved joint fires for this mission?
Exception: the approved fires for that mission are allowed.
An enemy in it is engaging a friendly force: does its commander need immediate protection?
Exception: respond with only the minimal force needed to defend the force.
No fires: fires or their effects are prohibited in a no-fire area.

slides.title: How an air support request moves up the chain

steps.label: Find a need for air support
steps.detail: When targets need effects beyond the unit's own capabilities, the fire support element creates an air support request.

steps.label: Send it to next higher headquarters
steps.detail: Fire support elements at each echelon send their requests to the next higher headquarters for approval.

steps.label: Each echelon reviews and merges
steps.detail: Approve or deny, verify priority, re-prioritize when needed, merge into a single air support list, and forward it.

steps.label: Senior Army headquarters decides
steps.detail: It adjudicates the requests and may add more in time for the joint targeting and air tasking cycles.

steps.label: Battlefield coordination detachment
steps.detail: The senior Army headquarters submits the list to the battlefield coordination detachment, which submits it to the joint air component.

steps.label: Air missions on the tasking order
steps.detail: Preplanned requests may result in scheduled and on-call air missions on the air tasking order.

slides.title: Field Artillery Operations

blurb.text: Field artillery destroys, neutralizes, or suppresses the enemy with cannon, rocket, and missile fire, and helps bring all fire support together.

slides.title: Five requirements for accurate first-round fire for effect

cells: Accurate target location and size
Detect, identify and locate the target; know its size and how it is spread out
Accurate firing unit location
Know where each weapon is, using survey and on-board navigation systems
Accurate weapon and ammunition information
Muzzle velocity, projectile weight, fuze type and propellant temperature
Accurate weather (meteorological) information
Firing data must compensate for weather effects on the projectile in flight
Accurate computational procedures
The computation of firing data must be accurate

talking_points.text: The goal of any indirect firing unit is accurate first-round fire for effect: fire meant to get the desired result on the target.
If the requirements cannot be met completely, the firing unit may be required to use adjust-fire missions.
Adjust-fire missions can mean less effect on the target, loss of surprise, more ammunition used and a greater chance of being detected.

slides.title: Four support relationships: who the artillery fires for

cells: Direct support
One specific force; answers that force's requests for help directly
Supported unit, then own observers, then field artillery headquarters (HQ)
Reinforcing
Another field artillery unit; adds to that unit's fires
Reinforced field artillery unit, then own observers, then field artillery HQ
General support-reinforcing
The force as a whole first; second, reinforces another field artillery unit
Supported unit, field artillery HQ, reinforced unit, then own observers
General support
The force as a whole, not any one part of it
Supported unit, then force field artillery HQ, then others (see table 4-1)

talking_points.text: Direct support is the most decentralized support relationship.
General support gives the highest degree of centralized control of fires.
Field artillery HQ is on the list only if designated by the support commander.

slides.title: Calls for fire: digital and voice

points.text: The field artillery battalion mainly uses digital means to plan and execute fires.
Whenever possible, digital fire missions should be rehearsed along the entire data link.
Voice may be necessary for unplanned, immediate fire requests or during denied, disrupted or degraded operations.
Fire direction centers (FDCs) must anticipate the circumstances and types of voice missions they may encounter.
Missions from untrained observers must be rehearsed during training.
The tactical solution and effects on the target should be essentially the same, voice or digital.

talking_points.text: FDC personnel receive calls for fire through the Advanced Field Artillery Tactical Data System or by voice.

slides.title: Global Positioning System (GPS) jammed? Get the signal back

steps.label: Use anti-jamming equipment
steps.detail: This is the best solution, if it is available.

steps.label: Block the signal
steps.detail: No anti-jamming gear? Put a barrier, such as your body, between the GPS device and the suspected jamming source.

steps.label: Pivot slowly
steps.detail: Using your body? Slowly pivot 90 degrees every two minutes until the signal is regained. The jammer is then behind you.

steps.label: Or put it in a hole
steps.detail: Or place the receiver in a hole six inches deep. A vehicle hatch may be used as a hole. Allow two minutes to get the signal.

steps.label: Still jammed? Move.
steps.detail: If neither technique works, move. The jammer is too close for these techniques to have any effect.

talking_points.text: Units must be prepared and trained to do the mission without GPS, using inertial navigation, maps, aiming circles and compass.
If digital communication is lost or degraded, it must be reestablished as soon as possible.
If one howitzer loses digital communications, the fire direction center will issue voice commands to it, or it can fire data from an adjacent section.

slides.title: Sun observations: protect your eyes

do.text: The sun filter should be inspected before use. Check that its coated surface is free from scratches or other defects.
If the sun filter is damaged or lost, a solar observation may be completed by the card method.
Card method: project the sun's image onto a card held 3 to 6 inches behind the eyepiece. Focus until the cross hairs are clear.

dont.text: The sun must never be viewed through the telescope without a sun filter.
Don't skip the precautions. Serious eye damage will result if proper precautions are not taken.

talking_points.text: Without GPS, field artillery personnel will use the M2A2 aiming circle for directional control. Soldiers can also use the sun and stars.

slides.title: Competition and Crisis

blurb.text: How fire support works before a war starts: during competition and during crisis.

slides.title: Fire support before the fighting: competition and crisis

points.text: An adversary pursues interests that clash with United States interests, but stays short of open armed conflict.
Fire support activities include security cooperation, training, maintaining readiness, and contingency planning.
At the tactical level, units will primarily conduct military engagement through combined training and exercises.
Activities to deter an adversary's undesirable actions, normally to keep competition from becoming military conflict.
The primary deterrent: a properly manned, equipped, and trained joint force that has shown it can prevail in large-scale combat.
Upon arrival in theater, units will conduct reception, staging, onward movement, and integration.

slides.title: Large-Scale Combat Operations

blurb.text: Fire support in large-scale combat: deep operations, the defense, the offense, and enabling, stability and reconstitution operations.

slides.title: Fire support in the defense vs. the offense

points.text: Counterpreparation fire: intensive, prearranged fire delivered when you discover the enemy attack is about to start.
Place fires in front of, on top of, to the side of, and behind obstacles to get the most out of them.
Plan targets, primary and alternate observer positions, and triggers for every engagement area.
Prepare and harden artillery and target acquisition positions, and rehearse on the actual terrain.
Field artillery units move well forward before an attack and displace by echelon to keep fires continuous.
To surprise the enemy, meet the five requirements for accurate predicted fire for first-round fire for effect.
Fire support coordination measures, such as coordinated fire lines, must be well forward so the force will not outrun them.
Forces forward of the forward line of own troops should have a restrictive measure, such as a no-fire area, to prevent friendly fire.

slides.title: Breaching fundamentals: suppress, obscure, secure, reduce, assault

steps.label: Suppress
steps.detail: Suppress enemy direct fire near the breach site. Suppression must also work against enemy indirect fire that can reach it.

steps.label: Obscure
steps.detail: Reduce enemy direct fire on breach and assault elements. Smoke should be used with fog or darkness; it may draw enemy attention.

steps.label: Secure
steps.detail: Mortars and field artillery keep suppressing and obscuring as needed while maneuver forces secure the breach site.

steps.label: Reduce
steps.detail: As maneuver forces with engineer support reduce the obstacle, mortars and artillery should keep suppressing, ready to lift or shift.

steps.label: Assault
steps.detail: As the force assaults through the breach, fires should continue, ready to lift or shift as it nears enemy battle positions.

slides.title: How terrain and weather change munitions and observing

cells: Deep snow (cold weather)
Airburst munitions; white phosphorous
High explosives (HE) point detonating or delay: ineffective in deep snow
Amber filters cut snow blindness; update visibility diagrams regularly
Rocky mountain ground
HE point detonating: splintering rocks add extra fragments
Swirling winds make smoke very hard to adjust and maintain
No laser rangefinder: looking up, you underestimate range; down, overestimate
Sandy or dune desert
Variable time and time fuzes are very effective
HE with point detonating or delay fuze is smothered by deep sand
Watch for dust clouds from moving enemy; heat waves hamper distance estimates
Triple-canopy jungle
HE-delay splinters trees for extra fragments; white phosphorous marks well
Smoke has limited effectiveness
Seeing beyond 25 to 50 m is very difficult; rounds often can't be seen
Urban areas
Fuze delay should be used to penetrate fortifications or building tops
Variable time fuzes may detonate early near other structures
FOs may be placed on upper floors; rooftop observers are vulnerable

talking_points.text: Forward observers (FOs) in the jungle must be able to adjust mortar and field artillery fire by sound, because often they cannot see the rounds.

slides.title: Hidden hazards in tough terrain and weather

items.text: Snow: white phosphorus may burn undetected for up to four days and may be a hazard to friendly troops moving through later.
Frozen lakes and rivers: determine ice thickness and load-bearing capacity before the field artillery crosses.
Dry riverbeds, wadis and gulches: positions there risk flash flooding.
Windows and other polished, flat surfaces may reflect laser energy and pose a hazard to friendly troops.
Elevators typically should not be used, so you don't get trapped if the power fails.
Weapons placed in buildings: collapse and fire are possible, and overpressure can significantly increase the noise hazard for crews.

talking_points.text: Rule of thumb: a minimum of 6 hours rest is required for every 24 hours without sleep.
In cold weather, panels or pyrotechnics must be used to indicate friendly locations.

slides.title: Key terms

terms.definition: Bringing together indirect fires, target acquisition, armed aircraft, and other attack systems against targets to support the commander's plan.
Fire delivered at a target the firing unit cannot see.
A mandatory call that warns of higher risk to the closest friendly troops from where a weapon impacts.
Killing or wounding friendly or neutral people by accident with friendly fire.
How the supported commander makes sure fires or their effects have no unintended consequences on friendly units or the scheme of maneuver.
An area set by the commander where fires or their effects are prohibited.
